content: Respiratory distress (RD) can occur in neonates born either preterm or at term, regardless of whether delivery is via normal vaginal delivery or caesarean section (CS). It is a significant cause of neonatal mortality, accounting for approximately 30% of neonatal deaths, and can manifest at any time after birth. The most common clinical presentations of neonatal RD include respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), transient tachypnoea of the newborn (characterized by rapid breathing), and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (marked by elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary vessels). Prostaglandins are routinely used in obstetric practice to prepare the uterine cervix and induce labor. Among the various types, prostaglandins of the E series are preferred due to their uteroselective properties. Administering prostaglandins to a pregnant woman before delivery facilitates the reabsorption of lung fluid from the fetal lungs and enhances surfactant secretion by triggering a catecholamine surge. This mechanism has the potential to significantly reduce neonatal respiratory morbidity following a CS, thereby decreasing the risk of long-term complications such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia (a chronic lung disease involving structural changes in lung tissue) and asthma. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether the administration of prostaglandins prior to CS improves respiratory outcomes in newborns. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of 30 September 2013) and three clinical trial registries, including ClinicalTrials.gov, the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, and the WHO Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), for ongoing studies (as of 24 June 2013). The review included all published and unpublished randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the use of prostaglandins with other treatments (including placebo) for reducing neonatal respiratory morbidity. The participants were pregnant women scheduled for CS, and the interventions compared were prostaglandin administration prior to CS versus no treatment, placebo, or alternative treatments. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion and evaluated their quality, with a third reviewer resolving any disagreements. Data extraction was performed by two reviewers and verified for accuracy. The Cochrane risk of bias tool was used to assess the included study, and study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. The review identified one RCT with a low risk of bias, conducted in a tertiary neonatal care center in Australia. This study involved 36 women, with 18 receiving intravaginal prostaglandin E2 gel and 18 receiving a placebo. In the control group, there was one case of neonatal respiratory distress, reported as transient tachypnoea of the newborn (risk ratio [RR] 0.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.01 to 7.68, one study, n = 36). None of the neonates in either group required mechanical ventilation. Median Apgar scores at one and five minutes were reported to be similar between the two groups. Additionally, no treatment-related side effects were observed in either group. The study reported significantly higher noradrenaline concentrations (median values and range) in the cord blood samples of the intervention group compared to the control group. The authors of the review concluded that, although the intervention group demonstrated a significant increase in catecholamine levels, there was no significant difference in respiratory outcomes between the intervention and control groups. The quality of evidence was graded as low due to the small sample size and the limited number of events. Consequently, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the effects of prostaglandins on neonatal respiratory outcomes based on this review.
